implementation_notes: Kotlin's coroutine context is itself a context object: a request-scoped value is modelled as a CoroutineContext.Element (a ThreadContextElement when it must also be installed into a thread-local while running), added with withContext(context) at the boundary and read from any suspending function via coroutineContext[Key]. Propagation follows suspensions rather than threads, so the value survives dispatcher switches without copying - and the element stays immutable per coroutine. The classic explicit request object is still the better choice when the value is genuinely a method argument in code that is not coroutine-based.
pitfalls: A context element is copied into child coroutines, not shared: rebinding it in a child is invisible to the parent, and a value set after a child was launched is not seen by that child.
A ThreadContextElement must be thread-safe and must restore exactly the state it saved in updateThreadContext, or an exception between resume and suspend leaves the thread-local stale.

variants.name: Ktor call.attributes with AttributeKey<T>
variants.implementation_notes: Server frameworks provide their own request-scoped map: in Ktor a plugin or interceptor stores per-call state in call.attributes under a unique typed AttributeKey<T>, and any handler downstream reads it back with the same key, so the ApplicationCall itself is the context object. This is the safer choice for data only the API layer needs, because the scope is exactly one call and nothing leaks into the coroutine context; use the coroutine-context element instead when lower, coroutine-based layers must see the value as well.
pitfalls: AttributeKey equality is identity-based, so two keys with the same name are different keys - the shared key must live in one place and be reused everywhere.
Attributes live for the whole call: holding large objects (bodies, buffers) there inflates memory per concurrent request and defeats streaming.
